question: Livestock farmers in the municipalities of Lokroi in Phthiotis and Orchomenos in Boeotia are still not receiving any meaningful support following the smallpox outbreak which struck last December, spreading through goat and sheep herds and leaving economic devastation in its wake. Veterinary authorities sought to contain the disease by killing all animals from contaminated farms.

In addition, the municipalities of Lokroi and Orchomenos have been declared restricted zones and the rest of the herds have been placed under mandatory quarantine. Almost five months have passed since the first case came to light, yet no measures have been put in place to support and compensate farmers. The meagre compensation offered for animals that were killed has not yet been paid.

Furthermore, under Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, in the event that authorisation is given for the immediate slaughter of animals from the restricted areas, the offal collected from the slaughterhouses is considered an animal by-product and must be destroyed, which, in the context of Greek Easter, reduces demand for the slaughterhouses in question.

The situation livestock farmers are facing is dire and there is uncertainty over whether they will be able to harvest a new fodder crop. In view of this: What is the Commission’s position concerning justifiable calls for: (a) full compensation for the losses incurred by livestock farmers who lost their animals and replacement of lost income by the State; (b) financial support (for fodder, disinfectants, etc.)
for livestock farmers who were forced to quarantine their animals and (c) the smooth-running slaughter of healthy animals coming from the restricted areas?
answer: Effective control of sheep pox and goat pox requires the establishment of protection, surveillance and further restricted zones, in line with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 (1) and Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/2725 (2).

Due to the infectivity and persistence of the disease, these zones must be of sufficient size and duration, so that no new outbreaks occur after control measures have been lifted. Fresh meat from sheep and goats kept in the protection and surveillance zones may be moved to other parts of the country only after the removal of offal, to prevent disease spread to disease-free areas.

In accordance with Regulation (EC) No 2021/690 (3) and Commission Implementing Decision C(2022)3467 [and amendments thereof: C(2023)1113 and C(2023)2280] (4), control measures implemented by Greece against outbreaks of sheep pox and goat pox in its territory, such as culling of affected animals, disinfections of holdings, etc., are eligible for EU co-funding, at a rate of 30%.

The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) also offers support to farmers. It can finance investments for the prevention and protection of livestock against communicable diseases, as well as for the restoration of production capacity on agricultural holdings damaged by, among others, communicable diseases in livestock. It also provides support to enhance on-farm biosecurity.

In addition, support concerning damages to livestock could be provided by the Hellenic Agricultural Insurance Organisation (ELGA), the central insurance coverage body for agricultural holdings in Greece, on condition that damages could be eligible for funding under the ELGA’s Regulation on Insurance of Livestock Capital.
